extracted.intended_audience: poets, students of poetics and rhetoric, and writers concerned with poetic diction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and refining poetic diction: defines the elemental parts of diction (letters, syllables, nouns, verbs, articles, conjunctions, case, discourse) and gives prescriptive guidance on noun-formation, phonetic qualities, and especially the types and selection of metaphors for poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet examines parts of diction not to teach correctness (as the grammarian does) but to render discourse more polite, soft, and harmonious and to imitate by words the nature of the things spoken of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetical study of diction focuses on shaping words to achieve politeness, softness, harmony, and imitation of nature; knowledge of the first elements (letters, syllables, words) is necessary for this poetic end. (Remarks: grammarian vs poet distinction; the poet uses diction to embellish and imitate rather than merely to conform to rule.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Eight parts of diction (core inventory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction properly speaking comprises eight parts: Letter, Syllable, Conjunction, Noun, Verb, Article, Case, and Speech (Oration/Discourse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These eight parts are the foundational elements a poet must understand; subsequent rules and aesthetic choices about sound, meaning, and arrangement proceed from mastering these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter — definition and requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A Letter is an indivisible sound which is articulate and intelligible — i.e., a sound by which we can understand signification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish letters from mere sounds (e.g., animal cries). A letter must be an elemental, indivisible unit used to form words; this is a basic requirement for any consideration of poetic sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters divided into vowels, demi-vowels, and mutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters are divided into Vowels, Demi-Vowels, and Mutes: a Vowel can make an intelligible sound alone; a Demi-Vowel borrows the voice of a vowel to be understood (often requires a preceding vowel); a Mute requires the addition of another letter with sound (a vowel) to be pronounced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand these roles when composing verse: which letters can stand alone, which need adjacency to vowels, and how consonantal behavior affects pronunciation and euphony (examples and letter lists provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of letters and syllables (quantity and accent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters/syllables differ by articulation (conformation of mouth), harshness/sweetness, short or long quantity, and accent (acute raises, grave falls, circumflex keeps even).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These qualities primarily concern versification and pronunciation; poets should study them (in treatises on verse) to place sweet or sharp tones and appropriate accents for euphony and metrical effect. Note: some details (aspirates, etc.) are language-specific (Greek) and may not apply elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllable — composition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: A Syllable is a sound which in itself signifies nothing and is composed of a Mute and a Vowel; monosyllables that signify (e.g., 'lux') are treated differently (often as nouns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syllable composition matters for versification and meter: when constructing poetic lines, pay attention to how syllables are formed (mute + vowel) and how quantity and accent interact with meter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunction — function and ornamental use
rubrics_metrics.description: A Conjunction is a sound that signifies nothing on its own and serves to join words that have their proper signification, making them one and the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjunctions can occur at the beginning, middle, or end of discourse. In poetry, including or omitting conjunctions is an ornament: adding them unites many into one, omitting them can make many out of one — use deliberately for rhythmic and rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article — prepositive and subjunctive roles
rubrics_metrics.description: An Article is a sound signifying nothing in itself but serves to show the beginning (prepositive, e.g., 'the') or end (subjunctive) of a discourse, or to separate one thing from another (e.g., 'I say', 'or to this subject').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles help point out referents and prevent the auditor's confusion; poets should use them to mark discourse boundaries and clarity. Note language differences (e.g., Latin lacks a definite article and uses demonstratives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Noun — definition and morphological types
rubrics_metrics.description: A Noun is a compounded sound that signifies something without denoting time; compounded parts of a noun (in many cases) signify nothing alone. Nouns can be simple, double, triple, quadruple, proper, foreign, metaphorical, ornamental, invented, protracted, subtracted, or changed; they also have gender (masculine, feminine, neuter) with characteristic endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets may use a wide range of noun-formation strategies (compound nouns, foreign borrowings, invented words, lengthening or shortening syllables, partial recomposition) to achieve effects; be aware of language-specific conventions and the aesthetic consequences (e.g., triple compounds suited to dithyrambic Greek but often inappropriate in Latin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb — definition, temporality, and cases/mood
rubrics_metrics.description: A Verb is a compounded sound which signifies something and (unlike a noun) determines time — e.g., 'he goes' vs 'he hath gone'. Verbal 'cases' here mean different inflexions corresponding to mood/intonation (indicative, imperative, optative) and are expressed by tone/gesture in speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use verbal forms deliberately to mark temporal relations and mood; recognize that verbs carry temporal and modal information important for narrative and dramatic effect (and that languages differ in how they mark these categories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case/Cadence — marking relation and number
rubrics_metrics.description: A Case (termination) in nouns and verbs marks sequel/relation and number (e.g., singular/plural) and can give words a wider sense than in languages without cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how case endings affect relationships among words in a line; poets working in or translating from case-marking languages must attend to these terminations to preserve syntactic and rhetorical relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oration/Discourse — unity and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: An Oration (discourse) is a compounded sound signifying something whose parts, though separable, retain meaning; an oration can be 'one' either by signifying a single thing or by composing several connected parts into one body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose discourse for unity either by clarity of single focus or by coherent connexion of several parts; recognize that a discourse need not be only nouns and verbs — some parts may have meaning independently (vocatives, exclamations), and poets exploit this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor — definition and four kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: A Metaphor is the transference of a noun from its ordinary signification. Four kinds are distinguished: (1) from Genus to Species, (2) from Species to Genus, (3) from Species to Species (resemblance), and (4) analogical metaphors (proportional relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate kind for rhetorical effect; many common metaphors are synecdoches (genus<->species), but the finest are analogical metaphors which rest on proportion and relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer analogical metaphors; invertibility and affinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical metaphors are the finest and should be chosen when possible; they require two conditions: (1) they must be invertible (the terms can be transposed and still correspond), and (2) they must be grounded on things of the same nature and kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting metaphors, check that the proportional relations hold both ways (inversion) and that the compared domains are of comparable kind; examples: 'old age is the winter of life' (invertible), 'cup of Mars' examples for personified possession. Avoid metaphors that cannot be plausibly inverted or that force dissimilar domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of foreign nouns as an elevation strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign (borrowed) nouns elevate diction and give majesty or an appearance of novelty — they please by resembling the pleasure we take in seeing strangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ foreign borrowings judiciously to exalt diction, but be mindful: inability to distinguish or explain foreign terms (or overuse) can reduce reader pleasure and comprehension. Historical note: Greek used many foreign terms; Latin and vernacular languages often less so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invented, protracted, subtracted, and changed nouns (poetic coinage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets may coin invented nouns; protracted nouns lengthen a vowel or add syllables; subtracted nouns lose a syllable; changed nouns recombine halves (half old, half new).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such manipulations are legitimate poetic devices for creating novel effects or adjusting sound/fit to meter. Use them with awareness of morphological plausibility and audience tolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperative mood as prayer or invocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperatives are not always formal commands; grammarians note that imperatives can function as prayers or expressions of necessity/confidence (as when speaking to the gods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking deities or making appeals, the imperative form can be used to convey urgency, necessity, or confident entreaty; poets should exploit this nuance rather than assuming all imperatives are commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language-specific phonetic transformations (aspirates, sweet/middle consonants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain phonetic changes (aspiration, sweet/middle consonant distinctions, transformations like b→p→ph, g→k→ch, d→t→th) are of great use in Greek and affect rhythm and sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that phonetic devices and permissible transformations are language-specific; rules or devices useful in Greek may be irrelevant or inapplicable in other languages, so adapt phonetic considerations to the target language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in extreme compounds (licentiousness varies by genre/language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Triple and quadruple compound nouns occur in dithyrambic Greek and express a licentious, elevated style; such forms were condemned in Latin style as inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match morphological daring to genre and language conventions: what is acceptable and effective in one poetic tradition may be frowned upon in another. Use highly compound forms only where stylistic context warrants.
